title: Praise
hookLine: say what's good about someone out loud
tomorrow: why does a son's rehearsed speech lose its last line?

lines: A TOAST, A SPEECH, A COMMENT.
cards: A toast at a retirement party. A speech at the end-of-season banquet. A comment under a friend's post.
Saying something good about someone, out loud, in front of people, can be strangely hard. Luke tells about a man who was praised twice without ever being in the room.
In Capernaum, Jewish elders hurry to Jesus with a request from a Roman officer, a centurion, whose servant is dying.
They plead his case, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "he loveth our nation; and he hath built us a synagogue." Jesus goes with them. Then, near the house, a second message arrives…

teach.b: …from the centurion himself, carried by friends: "Lord, trouble not thyself; for I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof." Just say the word, he adds. He's a man under orders; he knows how a word works.
Luke says Jesus marveled. Then he does something easy to miss.
He turns around to the crowd following him and says it out loud: "Amen I say to you, I have not found so great faith, not even in Israel." The servant is healed. Look at how the praise travels.

teach.h: PRAISE THAT NAMES WHAT WAS DONE.
teach.b: Jewish elders praise a Roman, an outsider, by naming exactly what he did. Then Jesus praises him again, in public, to a crowd that may not have expected it. Neither praise is vague.
The elders could have said he's a good man; they said what he built, and for whom. Neither is flattery; the centurion isn't even there to hear it.
And his own humble words stayed: Catholics echo them at Mass, just before Communion. Paul asks Christians to build one another up.
Praise is one of the plainest ways to do it: the good thing you noticed, named specifically, said where others can hear.

how: Before Communion at Mass, Catholics echo the centurion's words of Luke 7:6–7, and the Church's tradition of honoring saints is, in part, praising out loud the good that people did.

o: flattering a boss to get ahead
saying the good in someone out loud
a song only sung in church on Sunday

games.q: the centurion's afternoon — tap the pairs.
p: so great faith, not even in Israel

s: Jesus praises the centurion's faith out loud to the crowd
turning about to the multitude: I have not found so great faith, not even in Israel.
the centurion was a Jewish leader in Capernaum
a Roman officer; Jewish elders came to Jesus on his behalf.
praise means flattering someone so they'll like you
the centurion wasn't even there to hear it. the elders named what he'd done.

games.q: at your cousin's graduation party, everyone toasts the graduate. your quiet uncle, who drove her to every early practice, never gets mentioned. what would Luke's story do?
o: say out loud what he did, in front of everyone.
thank him privately later so he isn't embarrassed.
toast only the graduate; it's her day, not his.
games.why: Jesus didn't praise the centurion quietly; he turned to the crowd. and the elders praised by naming exactly what was done.

practice: Take a pen and write one sentence of praise about someone you know. Make it specific, the way the elders said he built us a synagogue, not just that he's great. Start with what they did, not what they are.
Read it back slowly, until it's ready to be said out loud where they, and others, can hear it.

wordCard.voice: Praise. Saying the good in someone out loud, specifically, where others can hear it, the way Jesus turned to the crowd.

orig.note: Latin: Lord, I am not worthy. the centurion's words, echoed before Communion.

carryVoice: Your line: say the good. The elders named what he built, and Jesus said it to the whole crowd. See you tomorrow.
